day.day_focus: Luke 15:3-4 - All the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near Him to listen to Him

scripture.text: So He told them this parable, saying, “What man among you, if he has a hundred sheep and has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open pasture and go after the one which is lost until he finds it?

exposition.text: Luke 15:3-4 opens with a scene marked by mercy that welcomes the very people religious pride keeps at a distance. The text does not ask the reader to admire the moment from a distance. The passage puts one clear scene in front of us: All the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near Him to listen to Him. We should stay with that scene before we rush to a slogan. What the passage shows through all, tax, collectors must be received before it is applied. That keeps the reading honest. the mercy of Christ receives sinners openly and exposes the coldness of self-righteous grumbling. Luke 15:3-4 stays concrete through So He told them this parable saying — the specific language of all, tax, collectors does the work before any principle is named. What Luke 15:3-4 puts before the reader is not abstract: all the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near him to listen to him. The text does not explain the scene from a distance — it names what people do when Jesus is near. The point is not bare information. It presses into faithful response instead of vague admiration. We should not drift into generic encouragement detached from the scene. We should let the passage name the pressure point for the day. If the scene is shaped by All the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near Him to listen to Him, then obedience today should answer that same pressure point. Where the text exposes fear, we should answer the word with concrete obedience. Where it honors devotion, we should practice glad nearness to Christ that welcomes repentant sinners instead of guarding respectability through distance. Where it reveals Jesus clearly, we should pursue steady trust in the ordinary places of life rather than delay. That keeps the day under the authority of Scripture. Strong exposition stays close to the text. It does not chase a clever slogan. It lets the details do their work on the conscience. That kind of reading slows us down. It teaches us to listen before we react. It also keeps prayer and application from drifting away from the passage. The passage sustains courage because Jesus remains worthy of trust in costly moments. The church's witness is strengthened when daily conduct aligns with confessed doctrine. The text rewards slow attention because its details are part of its theology, not background decoration. Good application therefore grows from disciplined reading rather than from devotional instinct alone. prompts: Sit with Luke 15:3-4 for two quiet minutes. Read the scene of mercy that welcomes the very people religious pride keeps at a distance slowly and let it settle before you move on.
Where does this passage call for glad nearness to Christ that welcomes repentant sinners instead of guarding respectability through distance today?
Stay for one more minute and answer God with one honest sentence of trust, repentance, or gratitude before continuing.

items: Write one sentence naming how Luke 15:3-4 presses on the scene of All the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near Him to listen to Him.
Name one place where glad nearness to Christ that welcomes repentant sinners instead of guarding respectability through distance should change the way you listen, speak, or act today.
action_steps.connector_phrase: Because Luke 15:3-4 calls for glad nearness to Christ that welcomes repentant sinners instead of guarding respectability through distance today:

prayer.text: Father, thank You for speaking clearly in Luke 15:3-4. In this passage You bring mercy that welcomes the very people religious pride keeps at a distance into the open through All the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near Him to listen to Him. Lord Jesus, keep us from reading these words as distant history only, and press them into our ordinary obedience today. Where we resist the truth highlighted in this reflection, bring repentance and renewed trust. Keep us near Your word, and do not let ordinary pressure turn us away from humble obedience. Holy Spirit, take what we have seen in the exposition and turn it into worship instead of mere information. Teach us to remember that Luke 15:3-4 opens with a scene marked by mercy that welcomes the very people religious pride keeps at a distance. Guard our speech from haste, our work from pride, and our choices from whatever would pull us away from faithful response instead of vague admiration. Amen.
